title: Ageing- and dementia-friendly design: theory and evidence from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology and environmental psychology can contribute to design guidelines that minimise spatial disorientation
central_proposition: Evidence from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, and environmental psychology can inform and improve ageing- and dementia-friendly design guidelines to minimize spatial disorientation by compensating for declining navigation abilities and leveraging residual skills.

concept_definitions.name: Wayfinding
concept_definitions.definition: The coordinated and goal-directed movement through the environment, defined as the process of determining and navigating a route from an origin to a destination.

concept_definitions.name: Landmark
concept_definitions.definition: Any object or feature of an environment that is easy to see and recognisable, especially one that helps to establish position.

concept_definitions.name: Egocentric strategies
concept_definitions.definition: Navigation strategies, also known as 'route' or 'response' strategies, that rely on associating a specific navigational or directional response with a particular landmark stimulus, and are rigid, inflexible, and unidirectional.

concept_definitions.name: Allocentric strategies
concept_definitions.definition: Navigation strategies, also known as 'place' or 'orientation' strategies, that rely on spatial representations (cognitive maps) independent of an individual's position, allowing for flexible route planning and shortcuts.

concept_definitions.name: Navigability
concept_definitions.definition: The extent to which various destinations can be reached with reasonable effort and within a reasonable time, related to good design for navigation.

concept_definitions.name: Differentiation
concept_definitions.definition: An environment's degree of visual or interior design features and spatial features that make elements like corridors or floors visually distinguishable.

concept_definitions.name: Visual access
concept_definitions.definition: The ability to see and recognize distant destinations and where one is headed within an environment.

concept_definitions.name: Layout complexity
concept_definitions.definition: The intricacy of a floor plan, characterized by factors like the number of route options, choice points, and corners.

argument_structure: The paper first reviews cognitive mechanisms of spatial navigation and how they are affected by typical and atypical (Alzheimer's disease) ageing. It then examines research from environmental psychology on design factors influencing indoor wayfinding. Finally, it integrates this psychological evidence with design knowledge to propose specific guidelines for ageing- and dementia-friendly environments aimed at minimizing spatial disorientation.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism involves compensating for age-related declines in spatial orientation and navigation abilities (e.g., impaired path integration, memory for landmark sequences, allocentric mapping difficulties) by optimizing environmental cues. This is achieved by designing environments that reduce cognitive load, enhance predictability, provide salient and unambiguous landmarks, and support residual egocentric navigation strategies, thereby facilitating recognition, orientation, and wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Age-related declines in wayfinding skills
findings.consequent: Difficulty learning to navigate in new, unfamiliar environments (e.g., sheltered housing, care homes)
findings.mechanism: Typical and atypical aging lead to marked declines in orientation and navigational abilities, making adaptation to novel surroundings challenging.
findings.quote: Age-related declines in wayfinding skills can make it difficult to learn to navigate in these new, unfamiliar environments.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Benke et al. 2014; Lester et al. 2017; Moffat 2009

findings.antecedent: Residential complexes designed to support spatial orientation and compensate for impaired navigation abilities
findings.consequent: Easier adaptation to new living environment for people with dementia
findings.mechanism: By reducing the cognitive demands of navigation, such designs allow individuals with declining abilities to better utilize their remaining skills and environmental cues.
findings.quote: Residential complexes that are designed to support spatial orientation and that compensate for impaired navigation abilities would make it easier for people with dementia to adapt to their new living environment.

findings.antecedent: Effective ageing- and dementia-friendly design
findings.consequent: Improved independence, quality of life, and well-being of residents, and reduced caregivers' workload
findings.mechanism: Facilitating navigation reduces stress and frustration for residents and caregivers, promoting autonomy and positive emotional states.
findings.quote: This would improve the independence, quality of life and well-being of residents, and reduce the caregivers' workload.

findings.antecedent: Spatial anxiety
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance in complex navigation tasks
findings.mechanism: Negative emotions consume cognitive resources, interfering with attention and memory processes critical for navigation.
findings.source: User-environment interactions in spatial navigation and wayfinding
findings.quote: spatial anxiety has a detrimental effect on wayfinding performance, particularly in complex navigation tasks

findings.antecedent: Sense of spatial self-efficacy and pleasure in exploring unfamiliar environments
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance
findings.mechanism: Positive motivational states enhance engagement and cognitive effort, leading to better learning and utilization of spatial information.
findings.source: User-environment interactions in spatial navigation and wayfinding
findings.quote: a sense of spatial self-efficacy and taking pleasure in exploring unfamiliar environments positively correlate with wayfinding performance

findings.antecedent: Small-scale environments (environmental aspect related to spatial navigation)
findings.consequent: Dysfunctional behaviour and improved well-being in people with dementia
findings.mechanism: Reduced spatial complexity and increased familiarity in smaller environments lower cognitive load and stress, promoting a sense of control and ease.
findings.source: User-environment interactions in spatial navigation and wayfinding
findings.quote: small-scale environments... are associated with the reduction in dysfunctional behaviour and improved well-being
findings.empirical_support_cited: Marquardt et al. 2014; Marquardt and Schmieg 2009

findings.antecedent: Landmarks with properties of uniqueness, saliency, persistence, informativeness, nameability, and relevant location
findings.consequent: Successful orientation and wayfinding
findings.mechanism: These properties ensure landmarks are easily noticed, recognized, remembered, and provide clear, unambiguous directional or positional information, reducing cognitive effort.
findings.quote: To be useful for the purposes of orientation and wayfinding, landmarks must have a number of properties
findings.empirical_support_cited: Nothegger et al. 2004; Raubal and Winter 2002; Stankiewicz and Kalia 2007a

findings.antecedent: Landmarks serving as associative cues ('turn right at the church') or beacons ('turn towards the church')
findings.consequent: Effective navigational information
findings.mechanism: Associative cues link actions to landmarks, while beacons provide direct visual targets, both simplifying route execution.
findings.quote: they can serve as associative cues if a movement in a particular direction is associated with a landmark ('turn right at the church'), or as beacons if they can be seen from the decision point
findings.empirical_support_cited: Waller and Lippa 2007; Wiener et al. 2013; Chan et al. 2012

findings.antecedent: Ageing
findings.consequent: Route learning ability (longer to learn novel routes)
findings.mechanism: Age-related neurodegenerative changes in the caudate nucleus, associated with route learning, impair the acquisition of new routes.
findings.quote: Cognitive ageing is associated with a decline in route learning ability
findings.empirical_support_cited: Head and Isom 2010; Hilton et al. 2021

findings.antecedent: Ageing
findings.consequent: Knowledge about the sequence in which landmarks were encountered along a route
findings.mechanism: Age-related cognitive decline specifically impairs the ability to encode and retrieve sequential information, even if individual landmark-direction associations are learned.
findings.quote: Typically ageing adults also show deficits in knowledge of the sequence in which they encountered landmarks along a route
findings.empirical_support_cited: Head and Isom 2010; Hilton et al. 2021

findings.antecedent: Ageing
findings.consequent: Efficiency in using allocentric navigation strategies (forming cognitive maps, planning new routes)
findings.mechanism: Deterioration of entorhinal-hippocampal circuits, crucial for allocentric navigation, impairs the ability to form and manipulate cognitive maps.
findings.quote: Healthy older adults also show deficits in using allocentric navigation strategies.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Iaria et al. 2009; Harris and Wolbers 2014; Liu 2011

findings.antecedent: Ageing
findings.consequent: Preference for egocentric navigation strategies over allocentric strategies
findings.mechanism: As allocentric abilities decline, older adults naturally shift towards less cognitively demanding egocentric strategies, which rely on familiar stimulus-response associations.
findings.quote: healthy older adults also tend to prefer different navigation strategies from younger adults
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wiener et al. 2013; Head and Isom 2010; Iaria et al. 2009

findings.antecedent: Ageing
findings.consequent: Difficulty switching from an egocentric to an allocentric navigation strategy
findings.mechanism: The cognitive flexibility required for strategy switching is impaired with age, particularly for the more demanding shift from a rigid egocentric to a flexible allocentric approach.
findings.quote: older people appear to have particular problems with switching from an egocentric to an allocentric strategy

findings.antecedent: Alzheimer's disease (AD)
findings.consequent: Spatial disorientation
findings.mechanism: AD-related neurodegeneration, particularly in the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus, directly affects brain areas critical for spatial orientation and navigation.
findings.quote: Spatial disorientation is one of the earliest signs of AD

findings.antecedent: Higher genetic risk of AD
findings.consequent: Navigation deficits
findings.mechanism: Subtle neurodegenerative changes associated with AD risk begin decades before clinical onset, impacting navigation circuits early.
findings.quote: adults at a higher genetic risk of AD show signs of navigation deficits decades before they may develop AD
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kunz et al. 2015; Coughlan et al. 2019

findings.antecedent: AD
findings.consequent: Impairments in hippocampal-dependent allocentric memory tasks (locating objects/landmarks relative to environment)
findings.mechanism: AD-related neurodegeneration primarily affects the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus, which are critical for allocentric spatial representations.
findings.quote: these effects seem more pronounced in spatial tasks that require a hippocampal-dependent allocentric memory
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kalova et al. 2005; Burgess et al. 2006

findings.antecedent: AD
findings.consequent: Translation between egocentric and allocentric representations
findings.mechanism: AD affects the retrosplenial cortex, which is involved in integrating and translating information between egocentric and allocentric reference frames.
findings.quote: AD has also been suggested to affect the translation between egocentric and allocentric representations

findings.antecedent: Environmental features (e.g., repetition of similar elements, symmetrical structures)
findings.consequent: Problems with orientation (harder to understand which part of a building one is in)
findings.mechanism: Low levels of spatial differentiation create ambiguity, making it difficult to uniquely identify locations and form distinct mental representations.
findings.quote: Low levels of spatial differentiation due to the repetition of similar elements or symmetrical structures, for instance—can give rise to problems with orientation

findings.antecedent: Symmetrical and harmonious structures
findings.consequent: Construction of cognitive maps
findings.mechanism: Gestalt principles like symmetry may facilitate the mental organization and representation of space, making the environment easier to comprehend as a whole.
findings.quote: symmetrical and harmonious structures facilitate the construction of cognitive maps

findings.antecedent: Limited visual access (e.g., too many corners)
findings.consequent: Difficulties with recognizing and locating distant destinations
findings.mechanism: Lack of clear sightlines prevents the formation of comprehensive spatial representations and hinders the use of beacons for navigation.
findings.quote: A limited visual access resulted in difficulties with recognising and locating distant destinations

findings.antecedent: Complex layouts (too many route options, choice points, corners)
findings.consequent: Negative navigation performance
findings.mechanism: Increased decision points and ambiguity overwhelm cognitive processing, leading to higher cognitive load and errors in wayfinding.
findings.quote: Complex layouts with too many route options, too many choice points along corridors, and too many corners... reportedly affected the students' navigation performance.

findings.antecedent: Small-scale units with good visual access
findings.consequent: Spatial disorientation
findings.mechanism: This layout makes spatial memory and recall, as well as wayfinding decisions, redundant, thereby reducing the cognitive load on impaired navigation abilities.
findings.quote: The reason why small-scale units with good visual access reduce spatial disorientation is that this layout makes spatial memory and recall, as well as way-finding decisions, redundant

findings.antecedent: Highly distinguishable private bedrooms and bedroom doors (e.g., portrait, name sign, memory boxes)
findings.consequent: Recognition and orientation for residents with dementia
findings.mechanism: Personalized and unique cues provide clear, meaningful landmarks that aid in immediate recognition and reduce confusion about one's own space.
findings.quote: recommend making private bedrooms and bedroom doors highly distinguishable to help with recognition.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Davis and Weisbeck 2016; Nolan et al. 2001, 2002

findings.antecedent: Communal spaces made easily recognizable and meaningful (e.g., landmarks, different furniture/color schemes, names)
findings.consequent: Support for navigation and orientation
findings.mechanism: Distinctive and meaningful features at decision points serve as effective landmarks, simplifying route choices and reducing cognitive load.
findings.quote: it makes sense for dementia-friendly design guidelines to place much emphasis on making places easily recognisable and meaningful
findings.empirical_support_cited: The King's Fund 2013; Davis et al. 2008

findings.antecedent: Corridors with clearly different design features (e.g., themes, colors, distinct entrances) visible from decision points
findings.consequent: Spatial disorientation in people with memory problems or dementia
findings.mechanism: Distinct features serve as beacons, enabling residents to use simple landmark-based navigation strategies that minimize memory load and compensate for impaired path integration.
findings.quote: corridors with clearly different design features that are visible from decision points could also serve as beacons, helping residents to use simple landmark-based navigation strategies that minimise memory load.

findings.antecedent: Brightly coloured, high-contrast objects (used as landmarks or navigational cues)
findings.consequent: Object recall and wayfinding for older adults and people with dementia
findings.mechanism: High contrast and saturation make objects more salient and easier to perceive and remember, especially for individuals with visual impairments or cognitive decline.
findings.source: Landmarks should be brightly coloured and feature high contrast
findings.quote: Objects that serve as landmarks need to be remembered and recognised. Older adults and people with dementia remember and recognise brightly coloured, high-contrast objects more easily than less-striking objects in pastel shades
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cernin et al. 2003; Gibson et al. 2004

findings.antecedent: Inappropriately placed or irrelevant colour cues
findings.consequent: Distraction for people with dementia
findings.mechanism: Irrelevant salient stimuli can divert attention from navigationally important cues, increasing cognitive load and potential for disorientation.
findings.source: Landmarks should be brightly coloured and feature high contrast
findings.quote: they are also particularly susceptible to being distracted by colour cues that are inappropriately placed or irrelevant

findings.antecedent: Landmarks or cues that are concrete and easy to name
findings.consequent: Verbal encoding of landmarks and support for navigation in dementia
findings.mechanism: Concrete, nameable objects facilitate verbal coding, which aids memory and recall, especially when language and word-finding problems are common in dementia.
findings.quote: to support the verbal encoding of landmarks, it is crucial to choose landmarks or cues that are concrete, rather than abstract... and therefore easy to name.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Meilinger et al. 2008; Grzeschik et al. 2018; Rohrer et al. 2008

findings.antecedent: Landmarks that are both visually and verbally distinguishable (e.g., different visual appearance AND different names)
findings.consequent: Confusion and disorientation
findings.mechanism: Ensuring distinctiveness across multiple sensory and cognitive channels prevents ambiguous mental representations that could lead to misidentification of locations.
findings.source: Landmarks should be both visually and verbally distinguishable
findings.quote: it is important to ensure that they are distinguishable in both domains... This could lead to confusion and disorientation, because the same mental representation would be associated with two different places.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Stankiewicz and Kalia 2007a; O'Malley et al. 2017

findings.antecedent: Landmarks located at decision points
findings.consequent: Memory for landmarks
findings.mechanism: Decision points inherently demand higher attentional engagement, leading to stronger encoding of associated landmarks and facilitating their use as navigational cues.
findings.source: Landmarks should to be placed at navigationally relevant locations
findings.quote: people navigating along a route remember landmarks that are located at decision points better than those located elsewhere along the route
findings.empirical_support_cited: Aginsky et al. 1997; Hartmeyer et al. 2017; Janzen and Tourennout 2004

findings.antecedent: Landmarks placed to serve as beacons (visible from decision points and guiding towards destination)
findings.consequent: Support for navigation in older adults
findings.mechanism: Beacon-based navigation is less memory-demanding than associative cue strategies, requiring only object recognition, which is relatively preserved in early dementia.
findings.source: Landmarks should be placed so that they can serve as beacons
findings.quote: Beacon-based navigation strategies are less memory demanding than associative cue strategies because we do not need to associate a direction of movement with the landmark
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wiener et al. 2013; Waller and Lippa 2007; Cushman et al. 2008

findings.antecedent: Signage containing both icons and text
findings.consequent: Understanding of navigation aids for people with dementia
findings.mechanism: Combining visual and textual information compensates for language and reading comprehension problems common in dementia, leveraging multiple processing channels.
findings.source: Signage should contain both icons and text
findings.quote: Signage should therefore not rely on textual information alone, but also contain pictures or icons... providing icons or pictorial information along with text on the same sign can greatly improve matters

findings.antecedent: Signage that is simple, uncluttered, and has clear contrast between text and background color
findings.consequent: Readability and comprehension for people with dementia
findings.mechanism: Reduced visual clutter and high contrast improve legibility and compensate for visual impairments associated with dementia, reducing cognitive effort.
findings.source: Signage should contain both icons and text
findings.quote: Signs should also be simple and uncluttered, preferably containing only one or two words... and... a clear contrast between the text and the background colour.

findings.antecedent: Signage using familiar, representational icons or pictorial information
findings.consequent: Comprehension of signs and icons for people with dementia
findings.mechanism: Familiarity aids recognition and understanding, while representational images are easier to process and recall than abstract ones, especially given memory decline in dementia.
findings.source: Signage should use familiar icons or pictorial information
findings.quote: familiarity is an important predictor of icon and symbol comprehension... it is also important for the icons used in signage for people with dementia to be representational rather than abstract.

findings.antecedent: Signage placed at eye level or lower (e.g., on the floor)
findings.consequent: Noticing and using signage for older adults
findings.mechanism: Older adults tend to look down while navigating to monitor locomotion and avoid hazards, making lower placement more likely to be seen and utilized.
findings.source: Signage should be placed where it can be seen
findings.quote: Older adults tend to look down whilst navigating... This has implications for the placement of landmarks and signage: to ensure they are not missed, they should be placed not high up on ceilings or walls, but at eye level or even lower.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Namazi and Johnson 1991; Liu-Ambrose et al. 2008

findings.antecedent: Personal environmental cues or features (e.g., relevant pictures, memorable spaces) in care homes
findings.consequent: Sense of being at home and wayfinding support
findings.mechanism: Personal cues foster a homely atmosphere, which is preferred over institutional signage, and can serve as meaningful, context-rich memory aids.
findings.quote: most of the care home residents interviewed in a recent study said they preferred more personal environmental cues or features, such as relevant pictures and memorable spaces, over signage or maps

findings.antecedent: You-are-here (YAH) maps with 'up' aligned with straight ahead in the real environment
findings.consequent: Cognitive effort needed to transfer map information to the real world
findings.mechanism: Aligning the map with the environment minimizes the need for mental rotation, a spatial ability affected by ageing, thereby reducing cognitive load.
findings.quote: it is important for YAH maps to be oriented so that 'up' on the map is aligned with straight ahead in the real environment... This minimises the cognitive effort needed
findings.empirical_support_cited: McKenzie and Klippel 2016; Zhao et al. 2019

findings.antecedent: YAH maps
findings.consequent: Useful navigation aids for people with dementia
findings.mechanism: Cognitive impairments in dementia, particularly memory and spatial reasoning, make it difficult to process and utilize abstract map information, leading to a preference for concrete landmarks.
findings.source: YAH maps may not be useful navigation aids for people with dementia
findings.quote: the available evidence suggests that maps in general, and even YAH maps, are of little use to them.
findings.empirical_support_cited: McGilton et al. 2003; Lanza et al. 2014

findings.antecedent: AD
findings.consequent: Ability to discriminate between colours, particularly in the blue and green range
findings.mechanism: Neurodegenerative changes in AD affect visual processing pathways, leading to specific deficits in color perception.
findings.source: Colour and contrast as design features to minimise spatial disorientation
findings.quote: AD affects people's ability to discriminate between colours, particularly in the blue and green range

findings.antecedent: AD
findings.consequent: Sensitivity to contrast
findings.mechanism: Visual processing deficits in AD reduce the ability to detect differences in luminance, requiring stronger contrast for objects to be noticed.
findings.source: Colour and contrast as design features to minimise spatial disorientation
findings.quote: people with dementia are less sensitive to contrast, which has to be stronger for them to notice it
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bassi et al. 1993; Cronin-Golomb et al. 1991; Crow et al. 2003

findings.antecedent: Lighter-coloured walls and less-contrasting furnishings
findings.consequent: Sense of spaciousness or confinement
findings.mechanism: Lighter colors and reduced contrast create an optical illusion of greater depth and openness, enhancing the perception of spaciousness.
findings.source: Colour and contrast as design features to minimise spatial disorientation
findings.quote: A sense of spaciousness can be enhanced by lighter-coloured walls and less-contrasting furnishings

findings.antecedent: Extra light and contrasting colours
findings.consequent: Ease of wayfinding for care home residents
findings.mechanism: Increased illumination and clear visual distinctions make environmental features more visible and recognizable, aiding orientation and navigation.
findings.source: Sufficient light levels and suitable colours are important to the creation of supportive environments
findings.quote: The use of extra light and contrasting colours can help care home residents find their way more easily

findings.antecedent: Personalising bedroom colours (based on stable preferences in AD)
findings.consequent: Care home residents' recognition of their own room
findings.mechanism: Leveraging stable personal preferences for colors creates a unique and familiar cue for individual rooms, aiding recognition despite cognitive decline.
findings.quote: personalising bedroom colours could be an effective way to help care home residents recognise their own room.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Design guidelines derived from cognitive and environmental psychology can be empirically tested for their effectiveness in reducing spatial disorientation in residential care and nursing homes.
The impact of specific landmark properties (e.g., uniqueness, saliency, nameability) on wayfinding performance in older adults and people with dementia can be quantitatively measured.
The efficacy of different corridor design strategies (e.g., themes, color differentiation) in minimizing disorientation can be evaluated through observational studies or controlled experiments.
The utility of signage combining icons and text, and its optimal placement, can be assessed through user performance and preference studies in dementia-friendly environments.
The effect of color contrast and light levels on object recognition and wayfinding in individuals with varying degrees of cognitive impairment can be experimentally determined.
bridge_warrants: Neuropsychological theories of orientation and navigation, backed by experimental evidence, can play a major part in improving the design of care environments.
Empirical evidence and neuropsychological theories can be used to develop improved ageing- and dementia-friendly design principles.
Interactionist models of ageing (e.g., person-environment fit, environmental docility hypothesis) highlight the importance of concurrently analyzing individual and environmental factors.
Knowledge from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, environmental psychology, and architectural design can be integrated to provide evidence-based guidelines.
methodological_critiques: Existing design guidelines and auditing tools for dementia-friendly environments often lack specific focus on alleviating disorientation and are not well supported by neuropsychological theories of navigation.

Wayfinding signage evaluations often rely on users' subjective perceptions rather than objective measurements of orientation and navigation performance, meaning existing guidelines may not be generally applicable.
model_structure: The paper does not propose a formal model but rather a framework for integrating psychological theories (cognitive, neuropsychological, environmental) with architectural design principles to create environments that compensate for declining navigation abilities in older adults and people with dementia.
limitations: The proposed approach has limits due to environments where changes cannot be implemented or navigation impairments are too severe.
The paper primarily focuses on Alzheimer's disease, limiting generalizability to other forms of dementia, although general age-related decline suggests broader applicability.
The guidelines are generic principles, requiring translation into bespoke solutions for specific environments.
Other factors beyond design (e.g., use of space, outside space, type of caring) also contribute to well-being but are not the focus of this paper.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractMany older people, both with and without dementia, eventually move from their familiar home environments into unfamiliar surroundings, such as sheltered housing or care homes. Age-related declines in wayfinding skills can make it difficult to learn to navigate in these new, unfamiliar environments. To facilitate the transition to their new accommodation, it is therefore important to develop retirement complexes and care homes specifically designed to reduce the wayfinding difficulties of older people and those with Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Residential complexes that are designed to support spatial orientation and that compensate for impaired navigation abilities would make it easier for people with dementia to adapt to their new living environment. This would improve the independence, quality of life and well-being of residents, and reduce the caregivers’ workload. Based on these premises, this opinion paper considers how evidence from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology and environmental psychology can contribute to ageing- and dementia-friendly design with a view to minimising spatial disorientation. After an introduction of the cognitive mechanisms and processes involved in spatial navigation, and the changes that occur in typical and atypical ageing, research from the field of environmental psychology is considered, highlighting design factors likely to facilitate (or impair) indoor wayfinding in complex buildings. Finally, psychological theories and design knowledge are combined to suggest ageing- and dementia-friendly design guidelines that aim to minimise spatial disorientation by focusing on residual navigation skills.
